topic: Binomial Distributions: Predicting Success in a Series of Trials
target_audience: High school or introductory-level university statistics students

sections.title: Prerequisite: The Bernoulli Trial
lecture_lines: Meet Lucky the Squirrel, our jump trial athlete.
Every jump has exactly two possible outcomes.
Success or failure; there is no middle ground.
animations: A white circle (#FFFFFF) labeled 'Lucky' appears.
A gap appears with the label 'Bernoulli Trial' at the top (#FFFF00).
Two arrows appear: Green (#00FF00) to 'Success (p)' and Red (#FF0000) to 'Failure (1-p)'.

sections.title: The Four Conditions (The BINS Criteria)
lecture_lines: To use a binomial distribution, check four criteria.
First: Is it Binary? Success or Failure only.
Second: Are trials Independent? One doesn't affect another.
Third: Is the Number of trials fixed?
Fourth: Is the Success probability the same each time?
animations: Vertical letters B, I, N, S appear in cyan (#00FFFF).
B: Binary - A lightbulb icon toggles yellow/grey (#FFFF00/#808080).
I: Independent - Two lightbulbs flash independently, no causal link.
N: Number - Row of 10 bulbs appears, labeled 'n=10'.
S: Same probability - Each bulb shows 'p=0.05' underneath.

sections.title: Deconstructing the Binomial Formula
lecture_lines: Let's break down the binomial probability formula.
n-choose-k counts all possible ways to arrange successes.
p to the k represents the success probability.
(1-p) to the (n-k) represents failure probability.
Together, they calculate probability for exactly k successes.
animations: Formula P(X=k) = nCk * p^k * (1-p)^(n-k) appears in white (#FFFFFF).
The nCk term turns cyan (#00FFFF) labeled 'Ways to arrange'.
The p^k term turns green (#00FF00) labeled 'Success probability'.
The (1-p)^(n-k) term turns red (#FF0000) labeled 'Failure probability'.
The full formula pulses once to show mathematical unity.

sections.title: Visualizing the Distribution (The Histogram)
lecture_lines: We can visualize probabilities using a histogram.
The bars show the likelihood of each outcome.
Changing n or p shifts the distribution's shape.
With p at 0.5, the distribution is perfectly symmetric.
High or low p values create a skewed graph.
animations: White axes (#FFFFFF) with labels 'k' and 'P(X=k)' appear.
Grey bars (#808080) of varying heights appear on the axes.
The bars change heights smoothly to show different probability distributions.
The bars align into a symmetric bell-shape in cyan (#00FFFF).
The bars shift to the left in red (#FF0000) then right in green (#00FF00).

sections.title: Calculation and Real-World Application
lecture_lines: The mean is the expected number of successes.
Multiply trials by success rate for the center.
This predicts risks in biology and engineering.
animations: Formula E(X) = n * p appears in yellow (#FFFF00).
Calculation '20 * 0.8 = 16' replaces the formula variables (#FFFFFF).
Distribution chart peaks at 16 with a highlighted bar (#00FFFF).
